## Original Research Article

The local field trial sample yielded encouraging results in terms of uptake of toxic elements.

The husk was removed from the sample of locally grown rice, and the brown rice was washed with deionized water and ovendried at 65 8 C. All samples were ground to a fine powder for analysis using a Fritsch Pulverisette 2 automated agate mortar and pestle (Fritsch, Germany). Samples were prepared for analysis by ICP-OES, F-AAS and TXRF by acid digestion. 20 mL of 1:3 HCl:HNO3 (Fisher TraceMetal Grade acids; Fisher Chemical, MA, USA) was added to 1 g of sample in a 70 mL graduated polyethylene vial, covered with a polyethylene watch glass and allowed to stand overnight. The following day the samples were digested at 110 8 C for 2 h using a graphite heating block (ModBlock; CPI International, CA, USA) and made up to 50 mL with 2% HNO3 (Howe et al., 2005).

The analytical techniques used were flame atomic absorption spectrophotometry (F-AAS) using a PerkinElmer 5100PC Spectrophotometer (PerkinElmer, MA, USA); inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) using a PerkinElmer Optima 7000DV (PerkinElmer, MA, USA); instrumental neutron activation analysis (INAA) using a SLOWPOKE II research reactor (Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, ON, Canada); and total reflection X-ray fluorescence (TXRF) using a Wobistrax /C223 TXRF spectrometer (Atominstitut der O ¨ sterreichischen Universita ¨ten, Vienna University of Technology, Vienna, Austria). The technique selected for each element was dependent on availability at the institution, detection limit and robustness.

Measurements by AAS and ICP-OES were done in triplicate, with the mean results being presented. The uncertainty of the measurements by INAA and TXRF are a function of acquisition time.

Calibration standards for F-AAS and ICP-OES analyses were prepared using Certiprep solutions (SPEX Certiprep, NJ, USA) in 2% HNO3. Deuterium lamp background corrections were performed for AAS. An internal standard containing 0.04 mg/L scandium and 0.2 mg/L yttrium was used for ICP-OES analyses.

For analyses using TXRF, the calibration and internal standards were prepared by serial dilutions of a solution containing 10,000 mg/L (Certiprep solutions) in 5% HNO3. An aliquot of a cobalt (Co) solution was added as an internal standard to achieve a final concentration of 10 mg/L. The samples were then homogenized with a vortex mixer and analyzed after pipetting 10 m L onto a quartz sample carrier/reflector and evaporating the solvent on a hot plate at low power.

The samples were irradiated under vacuum for 1000 s at 50 kV and 40 mA in a Wobistrax /C223 TXRF spectrometer (Streli et al., 2004). Blanks were treated identically to the samples.

INAA was performed using the SLOWPOKE-2 nuclear reactor. For the determination of short-lived radioisotopes, approximately 700 mg of sample was weighed out into pre-cleaned double polyethylene bags and heat sealed in pre-cleaned 7 cm 3 polyethylene vials (Lalor et al., 2000).

Each sample was irradiated for 3 min at a neutron flux of 5 /C2 10 11 n cm /C0 2 s /C0 1 and allowed decay periods of approximately 5 and 60 min before counting. For intermediate and long lived radioisotopes approximately 1300 mg of sample was weighed out in pre-cleaned polyethylene capsules which were then heat sealed in 7 cm 3 polyethylene vials and irradiated for 4 h at a neutron flux of 1 /C2 10 12 n cm /C0 2 s /C0 1 and allowed a decay period of 4 days and 14 days respectively before counting. For short and intermediate-lived radioisotopes gamma ray spectroscopy was performed using an Ortec High-Purity germanium coaxial gamma photon detector system with an efficiency of 71% and a resolution of 1.8 keV at the 60 Co 1332 keV gamma line. Dietary intake estimates were calculated assuming a body weight of 70 kg for males and 65 kg for females, and an average per capita consumption of rice by Jamaicans estimated at 71.2 g/day, based on a rice supply quantity of 26.0 kg/person/year (FAOSTAT, 2007).

## 2.1. Quality control

Approximately 10% of the samples were analyzed in duplicate, with the differences between duplicates being less than 15%; at least one reagent blank and a certified reference material were also included in each analysis batch.

Reference materials used were NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology, MD, USA) 8436 -Durum Wheat Flour, NIST 1568a -Rice Flour, NIST 1547 -Peach Leaves, NIST 1570a -Spinach Leaves, and IAEA (International Atomic Energy Agency, Vienna, Austria) 336 -Lichen. Reference material data are presented in Table 1.

For most elements the relative standard deviation of duplicate analyses was less than 10%, with a few (Al, Mo, S, U) having RSD between 10 and 20%; elements with RSDs greater than 20% were those which approached the detection limit of the technique (Ca, V, Ba, Sb, Sm). The agreement between techniques was excellent. Recovery for all reference materials used (were within acceptable limits of /C6 15%.

Reference values were not available for B, Hf, Mo, and Ti in any appropriate reference materials. For B analysis by ICP-OES, the data was validated by the use of the internal standards (Sc, Y) and an independent B standard solution; the mean recovery was 95%. For the remaining elements, analyzed by INAA, validation was achieved by the irradiation and counting of single element standards (Certiprep) with identical geometry to that used for samples (Grant et al., 1998) employing the improved relative standardization method (Kennedy and St-Pierre, 1993). Recoveries were 96%, 95% and 98% for Hf, Mo and Ti respectively. The linear range for elements analyzed using F-AAS, ICP-OES and TXRF is low mg/kg to 10 3 mg/kg in the samples. Digested samples which were beyond the linear range were diluted to fall within the linear range and reanalyzed. The linear range for INAA is low m g/kg to 10 4 mg/kg. Detection Limits and linear ranges are shown in Table 2; INAA detection limits may vary (Howe et al., 2005).

## 3.1.

Toxic elements

## 3.1.1. Aluminum

The range of values for aluminum in white rice was 6.1023.4 mg/kg while the range for brown rice was 7.40-43.0 mg/kg. The mean values for white and brown rice were 9.30 and 14.7 mg/ kg, respectively. The maximum value of 43.0 mg/kg was found in the brown basmati rice brand. The bulk rice had 23.4 mg/kg and a brand of long grained parboiled rice had 15.6 mg/kg. A diet high in rice would not be expected to expose humans to toxic levels of aluminum, but it is of note that the preference in the Jamaican diet is bulk rice which has the second highest quantity of Al in the survey. Aluminum has not been shown to perform any essential function in humans (McDowell, 1992). There has been growing evidence of toxicity however and the World Health Organization revised the Provisional Tolerable Weekly Intake (PTWI) from 7 mg/ kg of body weight to 1 mg/kg of body weight in 2006 based on the conclusions that levels lower than the previous PTWI (Provisional Tolerable Weekly Intake) may affect the developing nervous and reproductive systems (JECFA, 2007). There have been several studies linking an accumulation of aluminum in the brain and Alzheimer's disease but no causal relationship has as yet been established (Frisardi et al., 2010).

The arsenic content of the white rice samples had a range of 0.110-0.487 mg/kg, while the range for brown rice was 0.0820.250 mg/kg. The mean arsenic content of the white rice samples was 0.20 mg/kg, and 0.165 mg/kg for brown rice. The highest sample measured, Roland Arborio rice from Italy, contained 0.49 mg/kg of arsenic. The likely source of arsenic is the water with which the paddies are flooded. Some arsenic compounds are used in herbicides and fungicides. A limit for arsenic in rice has not been established by CODEX; however the WHO has established a PTWI of 0.015 mg/kg bw for inorganic arsenic. Chronic arsenic overexposure results in clinical manifestations in almost every system of the body.

In July, one composite soil sample was collected from 4 points within the study area of each rice paddy, and in September, one composite sample of rice grain was harvested from 10 plants within each study area. In September 2009, one rice sample was collected near Wanshan, in eastern Guizhou province, China, where traditional /uniFB02 ooded irrigation methods were practiced (Fig. 1).

## 2.2. Laboratory methods

## 2.2.1. Sample preparation and preservation

In July, rice samples (roots, stems, leaves, and seeds) were rinsed with Milli-Q H2O, air-dried for 2 weeks, then freeze-dried and ground for analysis.

In September, rinsed rice samples (roots, stems, and leaves) were air-dried for about 2 months and then ground for analysis. The stainless steel grinder was cleaned with ethanol after each sample to avoid cross-contamination. In September, aqueous samples were collected in 100 mL borosilicate bottles, which were acid-cleaned (20% HNO3) and rinsed with Milli-Q H2O, followed by heating in an oven at 550 /C14 C to thermally desorb Hg. Filtered (0.22 m M) and un /uniFB01 ltered aqueous samples were immediately acidi /uniFB01 ed to 0.5% HCl at Tuanlin Experimental Station, and stored in a dark refrigerator (4 /C14 C). ## 3.2. HgT and MeHg concentrations in rice plants

HgT and MeHg concentrations for rice plants harvested in July and September are shown in Figs. 2 and 3.

In both months, mean leaf HgT levels were similar or higher than root HgT levels, which suggested stems were not the only source of HgT to the leaves. Findings were consistent with previous research that demonstrated leaf HgT was mainly accumulated from the atmosphere and not the roots (Ericksen et al., 2003; Rea et al., 2002; Stamenkovic and Gustin, 2009; Zhang et al., 2010d).

In July leaf HgT levels were signi /uniFB01 cantly higher in site 1 compared to sites 2 and 3 (ANOVA, p < 0.05, n ¼ 6) (site 1: 300 /C6 47 ng/g, site 2: 42 /C6 12 ng/g, site 3: 52 /C6 24 ng/g). Site 1 was located downwind from a cooking oil factory emitting pollution from a smokestack at the same time rice plants were collected, although atmospheric Hg was not measured. Site 2 was located upwind from the factory and Site 3 was further downwind (Fig. 1). The mean HgT value for leaves at site 1 (300 ng/g) was derived from rice plants collected in 2 paddies (leaf HgT paddy 1: 270 /C6 14 ng/g, n ¼ 2 replicates; leaf HgT paddy 2: 330 /C6 90 ng/g, n ¼ 4 replicates). In contrast to July, leaf HgT levels in September were similar at all 3 sites (one-way ANOVA, p > 0.05, n ¼ 6), which suggested HgT was not stored between July and September in the leaves. Higher accumulation of MeHg compared to HgT in rice grain was consistent with earlier studies that reported inorganic Hg(II) sorbed by roots was not readily translocated to the aerial portions of the plants (Beauford et al., 1977; Cavallini et al., 1999; Greger et al., 2005; Lindberg et al., 1979), and the proportion of MeHg was higher compared to inorganic Hg(II) in the aboveground plant biomass (Schwesig and Krebs, 2003). One hypothesis is that glutathione-derived peptides present in the roots, called phytochelatins (Cobbett and Goldsbrough, 2002), chelate inorganic Hg (II) more ef /uniFB01 ciently than MeHg, which was suggested by Krupp et al.

(2009). Limitation of inorganic Hg(II) translocation may be a protective mechanism since inorganic Hg(II) may hinder transpiration, affect plant growth, or cause oxidative stress (e.g., Zhou et al., 2007), and should be further tested.

## 3.3. Calculation of daily MeHg ingestion rate

The average rice ingestion rate in 2008 in China was 270 g/d, which was based on the annual total rice consumption (130,778 /C2 10 3 t, from IRRI, 2010) and the population of China (1,324,655 /C2 10 3 , from PRB, 2010).

Using the mean MeHg levels in white rice (average: 1.2 ng/g, n ¼ 12), and assuming mean body weight is 60 kg, the mean daily MeHg intake rate from rice ingestion was 0.0054 m g kg /C0 1 d /C0 1 , which was 17 times lower than the U.S. EPA recommended level (0.1 m g kg /C0 1 d /C0 1 , USEPA, 2001b). Higher MeHg exposure levels were reported for brown rice in the Hg mining area in China, assuming the daily rice ingestion rate was 620 g/d (e.g., 0.26 m g kg /C0 1 d /C0 1 from Qiu et al., 2008; 0.012 e 0.44 m g kg /C0 1 d /C0 1 from Zhang et al., 2010c). Using the higher ingestion rate, the daily MeHg exposure level for this study was 0.012 m g kg /C0 1 d /C0 1 (i.e., 8.1 times lower than the U.S. EPA reference dose, USEPA, 2001b), which indicated rice grain harvested from these paddies near Tuanlin village, Hubei province, China was not a signi /uniFB01 cant source of MeHg to humans.

Fish consumption is considered as the primary pathway of human methylmercury (MeHg) exposure. However, recent studies highlighted that, rice, rather than /uniFB01 sh, is the main route of human MeHg exposure in Guizhou, inland China. China is considered as the largest anthropogenic source of mercury (Hg) emission in the world, which has led to serious environmental Hg pollution.

But there are no comprehensive studies regarding this environmental health problem to evaluate human Hg exposure and associated health effects. This study aimed to estimate daily MeHg intake and health risk in 7 provinces in southern China, and to assess the relative contribution from rice and /uniFB01 sh consumption. The average levels of total mercury (THg) and MeHg in rice samples were generally low at 10.1 ng·g -1 and 2.47 ng·g -1 , respectively. But a total of 36 rice samples (12.7%) had THg concentration exceeding the national limit (20 ng·g -1 ). Generally, rural population had signi /uniFB01 cantly higher Probable Daily Intakes (PDIs) of MeHg than urban population from rice consumption and its relative contribution to MeHg exposure increased signi /uniFB01 cantly from coastal to inland area. The averages of PDIs of MeHg were 0.020 μ g·kg -1 ·d -1 and 0.028 μ g·kg -1 ·d -1 for urban and rural population in southern China, respectively. Despite the serious environmental Hg pollutions in China, the general population in southern China had low risk of MeHg exposure. But rice is an important route of human MeHg exposure in southern China, especially for the rural population in inland area. The /uniFB01 ndings indicate that rice consumption should be considered when evaluating MeHg exposure in rice eating population in southern China.

## 2.2. Analytical method

In the laboratory, the rice samples were air dried, crushed, and sieved to 150 meshes. For total mercury (THg) analysis, rice samples were digested in a water bath (95 °C) with a fresh mixed acid of HNO3:H2SO4 (4:1, v/v) (Horvat et al., 1991) and determined by SnCl2 reduction, purge, gold trap, and cold vapor atomic /uniFB02 uorescence spectrometry (CVAFS) detection according to USEPA Method 1631 (USEPA, 1999).

For MeHg measurement, rice samples were digested using the KOH-methanol/solvent extraction technique (Liang et al., 1994, 1996) and measured by aqueous ethylation, purge, trap, and gas chromatography (GC) coupled with CVAFS detection according to USEPA Method 1630 (USEPA, 2001). Detail information of quality control is available in the Supporting information.
